\section{Three Scenarios for the Lending Environment}
\label{sec:scenarios}

% Every number is read from thesis/chapters/generated/tab_scenarios.tex, tab_switches.tex,
% (both from results/raw/rq3s.parquet, 100 replicates per arm)
% tab_cooloff.tex or tab_cap.tex, or from results/summary/results_numbers.json, all generated by

This section answers RQ3.
We compare three scenarios, and a fourth arm that combines the two switches to test whether either changes the effect of the other.
The benchmark is the pre-2026 position, in which \ac{BNPL} obligations are invisible to the bureau and requests pass only a light screen.
Under bureau visibility ($\mathbb{1}^{\text{bur}}$), \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the traditional lender's Regulation 23A test. This is the affordability channel of the reported 2026 arrangements \cite{businessday_bnpl_2026}; the scoring channel is outside the model (Section~\ref{sec:asymmetry}).
Under mandatory affordability screening ($\mathbb{1}^{\text{aff}}$), the Regulation 23A test is applied to each \ac{BNPL} request, the South African analogue of the \ac{FCA}'s proportionate affordability check \cite{fca_ps26_1, woolard2021}.
Every arm is run at $\beta = 0$ and at $\beta = 1$ (Equation~\ref{eq:peer}), to test whether the results depend on how adoption spreads.

The light screen in the benchmark is a modelling assumption.
Whether an agreement that levies late fees is incidental credit, and which provisions would then apply, is a legal question that the scenarios do not settle (Section~\ref{sec:background}).

Table~\ref{tab:scenarios} reports the outcomes, Table~\ref{tab:switches} sets the two switches beside their combination, and Figure~\ref{fig:scenarios} plots default and cumulative volume.
These four arms have one hundred replications each on shared seeds, five times the number used elsewhere, because the differences between them are small.
Differences are scenario less benchmark at the same $\beta$, taken seed by seed, and carry one standard error.
We report cumulative volume beside default because a rule that only delays borrowing within the horizon leaves volume unchanged, whereas a rule that prevents borrowing lowers it.

Bureau visibility raises default, and screening does not change it detectably.
Bureau visibility raises default by $0.22 \pm 0.04$ points at $\beta = 0$ and by $0.15 \pm 0.04$ at $\beta = 1$.
Screening changes it by $+0.02 \pm 0.05$ and $+0.02 \pm 0.06$ points.
With both switches default is $0.10 \pm 0.05$ and $0.11 \pm 0.05$ points above the benchmark, each just beyond two standard errors.
The largest standard error among the six comparisons is 0.06 points, so screening may have an effect smaller than about 0.11 points, in either direction, that this design cannot see.

Bureau visibility acts through the traditional lender's refusals.
Once \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the Regulation 23A test, the lender refuses more applications, 1{,}388 against 1{,}190 at $\beta = 0$, and grants R4.97 million in place of R5.39 million.
The 90+ day arrears share among credit-active households rises by $0.42 \pm 0.05$ points at $\beta = 0$ and by $0.28 \pm 0.04$ at $\beta = 1$.
The rise in default is largest in Q1, at $0.59 \pm 0.07$ and $0.46 \pm 0.08$ points, and is not detectable in Q2 to Q4.
A household that the lender refuses leaves its shortfall unpaid and is recorded as distressed (Section~\ref{sec:amount}), which is consistent with these rises, although the aggregates do not show that the refused households are the ones that default.
Cumulative \ac{BNPL} volume is $2.6 \pm 0.6$\% lower at $\beta = 0$, although the switch does not act on \ac{BNPL} requests.

The model counts the cost of a refusal within a two-year horizon, gives a refused household no other source of credit, and assesses every application on surveyed income.
A loan that is granted postpones distress within the horizon, and its later cost may fall outside it.
The result therefore gives the direction of the affordability channel in the model and does not forecast the reporting arrangements.

Mandatory screening refuses \ac{BNPL} requests that the light screen would grant.
Holding at the final tick falls from 17.54\% to 15.69\% at $\beta = 0$ and from 66.74\% to 64.11\% at $\beta = 1$, and cumulative volume is $3.9 \pm 0.5$\% lower at $\beta = 0$ and $1.1 \pm 0.2$\% lower at $\beta = 1$.
The screening test already sees the household's \ac{BNPL} instalments on every platform (Section~\ref{sec:asymmetry}), so adding bureau visibility to screening gives the platforms no new information.
The addition acts on the traditional lender, which refuses 114 more applications than in the benchmark at $\beta = 0$, against 198 under bureau visibility alone.
At $\beta = 0$ default with both switches is $0.12 \pm 0.04$ points below default under bureau visibility alone; at $\beta = 1$ the two do not differ detectably.

Two features of the model may explain why default does not respond.
A \ac{BNPL} agreement is small beside the room that the Regulation 23A test allows: each platform limits a household to a tenth of its monthly income and the mean want-driven purchase is R633, so the test refuses only households already close to the limit.
The test also assesses affordability at origination on the household's surveyed income, whereas sustained distress in the model follows income shocks that outlast the household's buffer (Section~\ref{sec:results-robustness}).
A test applied when credit is granted cannot see a shock that arrives later.
Neither explanation is tested, because the outcomes do not follow the screened households.

Peer influence raises holding, volume and default in every scenario.
In the benchmark, holding at the final tick is 66.74\% at $\beta = 1$ against 17.54\% at $\beta = 0$, and cumulative volume is R65.90 million against R6.45 million.
Default is 0.53 to 0.61 points higher at $\beta = 1$ across the four arms.
The effect of bureau visibility is $0.07 \pm 0.06$ points smaller at $\beta = 1$ than at $\beta = 0$, which is not detectable, and the comparisons give no evidence that peer influence alters the effect of either switch.

Appendix~\ref{app:levers} reports two further levers, each run at both values of $\beta$ with twenty replications.
The first is a cooling-off window that blocks want-driven purchases for one to four ticks after a want-driven purchase (Table~\ref{tab:cooloff}).
The second is a cap on the number of platforms a household may owe, which is hypothetical because no jurisdiction imposes one (Table~\ref{tab:cap}).
A household at the cap is refused every new agreement until a balance clears, so a cap of one allows one agreement at a time.
At $\beta = 0$ neither lever changes default detectably, although a cap of one removes 40.1\% of volume.
At $\beta = 1$ the window lowers default by between $0.28 \pm 0.08$ and $0.39 \pm 0.12$ points, and caps of one and two lower it by $0.31 \pm 0.12$ and $0.32 \pm 0.10$ points.
Cumulative volume in these arms is between 31.8\% and 76.3\% lower.
A cap of three does not change default detectably.

Where a lever lowers default detectably, it also removes about a third or more of borrowing, and peer influence is present.
The experiments do not show that the lost volume is the cause.
In a diagnostic run at $\beta = 1$, a cap of two that counts agreements in place of platforms removes 32.9\% of volume and changes default by $-0.11 \pm 0.07$ points, which is not detectable (Appendix~\ref{app:levers}).
Bureau visibility and screening remove between 3\% and 5\% of volume at $\beta = 0$ and under 2\% at $\beta = 1$.
No lever was run under the alternative borrowing rules of Table~\ref{tab:effect}, so the dependence of these results on those rules is untested (Section~\ref{sec:amount}).
The model also has no measure of what a household loses when a purchase or a shortfall loan is refused.

In answer to RQ3, bureau visibility leads the traditional lender to refuse more applications and raises default by 0.15 to 0.22 points, mostly in the lowest income quintile.
Mandatory screening lowers \ac{BNPL} holding and volume and does not change default detectably.
These results bound only the channel modelled (Section~\ref{sec:lim-reading}).
